findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation presents substantial unknown risk to audit and financial governance position
findings.detail: The Council is due to be replaced by a larger local authority through LGR by 2028/29. External auditors and management acknowledge that the impacts of this restructuring on the audit position are not currently known. The Audit Committee explicitly noted LGR as representing a substantial area of risk.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change creates uncertainty about how financial accountability and audit will be managed post-reorganisation, affecting the trajectory of audit assurance recovery.
findings.figures: LGR anticipated by 2028/29; spans period when audit disclaimed opinions are expected
findings.quote: Fundamentally, it is not known what that the impacts of LGR will be on the Council's audit position at the current time. The Committee noted, therefore, that LGR represents a substantial area of risk.

findings.headline: Staff churn and control gaps: Internal audit upgraded from Limited to Moderate Assurance but with consistency and resilience concerns
findings.detail: Internal Audit opinion improved to Moderate Assurance (from Limited in 2024/25), but auditors found controls are not consistently applied across the organisation. Staff churn has created single points of failure risk, and succession planning is needed to embed recent control improvements and ensure long-term resilience.
findings.matters: Governance resilience is at risk if key staff leave; control inconsistencies could undermine financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Opinion upgraded from Limited Assurance (2024/25) to Moderate Assurance (2025/26)
findings.quote: churn in staff has emphasised risks around potential single points of failure, which should be mitigated against

findings.headline: External audit will issue disclaimed opinions for years due to unaudited historic period from Coronavirus pandemic
findings.detail: Disclaimed audit opinions are anticipated until after the 2027/28 audit because of an unaudited historic period in the Council's accounts from 2019/20 onwards. The external auditor cannot fill this gap within available capacity. The Council maintains its accounts are accurate and it holds sufficient reserves, but external audit assurance remains qualified.
findings.matters: A lender cannot obtain full external audit verification of the Council's financial position for at least two more years, relying instead on management assurance and disclaimed opinions.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions anticipated through 2027/28 audit; materiality threshold £1.2 million
findings.quote: it is anticipated that disclaimed opinions will be made until after the 2027/28 audit

findings.headline: Accounts Payable authorization failures persist despite S114 spending controls introduced in 2023
findings.detail: Following the Section 151 Officer's 2023 S114(3) report, Accounts Payable audit found continuing issues: vacation rule authorisations being misdirected and payments authorised by officers lacking appropriate delegation authority. No PO No Pay policy implemented June 2025 has reduced but not eliminated Retrospective Purchase Orders. Audit confirms S114 controls have not adversely affected payment timeliness but underlying authorization weaknesses remain.
findings.matters: Continuing payment authorization failures despite prior S114 intervention indicate persistent governance weakness; unauthorized payments represent ongoing financial control risk to the council.
findings.figures: Continuing vacation rule issues; Retrospective Purchase Orders still being required despite No PO No Pay policy implementation
findings.quote: Payments are being authorised by officers who do not have the appropriate levels of authorisation.

findings.headline: Accounts Receivable collection has deteriorated with 45.1% of debt over one year old
findings.detail: Accounts Receivable audit found 45.1% of total outstanding debt aged over 1 year, indicating ongoing recovery challenges. Substantial element relates to Adult Social Care land charges where recovery is uncertain and dependent on asset realisation. Some long-standing debts are beyond statutory recovery period, increasing unrecoverable income risk. Audit notes 'further review of aged debt is required to ensure debts with no realistic prospect of recovery are identified and written off in a timely manner.'
findings.matters: Aged debt at this level indicates deteriorated cash flow collection and represents material unrecovered income; debts beyond statutory recovery represent write-off risk and uncollectable assets on balance sheet.
findings.figures: 45.1% of total outstanding debt aged over 1 year; substantial proportion relates to Adult Social Care land charges
findings.quote: 45.1% total outstanding debt aged > 1 year, indicating ongoing recovery challenges.

findings.headline: Salary overpayments remain at £540k with no reduction despite new monitoring systems
findings.detail: Salary overpayments audit found persistent high levels totalling £540k (November 2025) with no reduction in occurrence. Weaknesses include weak policy compliance, extended recovery periods without proper approval, capacity constraints in Legal Services delaying recovery, inconsistencies between Legal and financial records, no central write-off register, and limited escalation to senior management. Root causes (late manager notifications) not effectively addressed despite new Power BI dashboard.
findings.matters: Persistent unrecovered overpayments of this scale indicate fundamental control weaknesses in a critical payroll function; lack of reduction despite new controls suggests the improvements are not addressing underlying causes.
findings.figures: £540k outstanding as of November 2025; one significant case of £20k highlighting ongoing weaknesses
findings.quote: High and persistent level of overpayments (As at November 2025, £540k outstanding) with no reduction in occurrence.

findings.headline: Direct Payments scheme (£18.9m budget) has control weaknesses with emerging financial and safeguarding risks
findings.detail: Direct Payments audit found approval arrangements inconsistent with Scheme of Delegation, limited segregation of duties with key responsibilities in single roles, over-reliance on small number of officers, and incomplete assurance over managed account provider (which lost FCA registration). Financial monitoring not completed quarterly due to resource constraints. Audit identified: 'Emerging financial and safeguarding risks... including accounts with no recorded payments, increasing personal contribution deficits, potential misuse of funds, and unresolved investigations.' Notes that despite compliance improvements, 'increasing contribution deficits and accounts with no recorded payments suggest a deterioration in some key financial and safeguarding risk areas.'
findings.matters: Weaknesses in a £18.9m scheme carrying direct financial and safeguarding risks, with identified deterioration in financial outcomes and over-reliance on individuals, expose the council to significant loss and regulatory action.
findings.figures: £18.9m Direct Payments budget; increasing contribution deficits; accounts with no recorded payments
findings.quote: Emerging financial and safeguarding risks were identified, including accounts with no recorded payments, increasing personal contribution deficits, potential misuse of funds, and unresolved investigations.

findings.headline: Capital Works Programme governance has significant weaknesses limiting effectiveness of control framework
findings.detail: Audit of the council's capital programme identified multiple control failures: lack of formal escalation mechanism for project variances, absence of formal year-end capital outturn review, single-point dependency in capital project financial oversight, limited budget oversight without formal documentation, and reduced lessons learned activities. The audit concludes the framework 'could become inadequate and ineffective in supporting the governance and successful delivery of the capital programme unless the identified improvements are implemented.'
findings.matters: Capital programme governance weaknesses directly impair the council's ability to deliver infrastructure commitments and manage capital borrowing effectively, affecting financial resilience and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Not specified; identified across capital works governance
findings.quote: Despite the existence of a centralised governance framework and established oversight arrangements, the audit identified weaknesses that collectively significantly reduce the effectiveness, consistency and resilience of capital programme governance.

The Council's financial resilience is dependent on delivery of the Transformation Programme savings, maintaining financial discipline across services, and stable funding assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025 - 2026
findings.headline: Financial forecasting accuracy is weak, evidenced by a massive gap between Exceptional Financial Support approved and actually required.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget included £41.024m of Exceptional Financial Support, but only £7.737m was required at year-end—a £33.3m forecasting error. This suggests the Council's budget planning and demand forecasting is unreliable.
findings.matters: A lender relies on forecasts of financial need, savings delivery and budget performance. A forecast error of this scale indicates material forecasting weaknesses.

findings.quote: The 2024/25 budget included £41.024m of Exceptional Financial Support; however, only £7.737m was required at year-end. This resulted in an underspend against the approved budget

findings.headline: External Audit has identified 'significant weaknesses across all three VfM criteria for the fifth consecutive year', indicating systemic governance, financial management and efficiency failures.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 Value for Money assessment identified significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, and economy/efficiency/effectiveness. Key issues include weaknesses in budget setting assumptions, delivery and transparency of savings, immature risk management, limitations in internal audit effectiveness, and ongoing challenges in procurement, ICT governance, and service improvement in Housing, Adults and Children's Services. Three new recommendations raised in 2024/25 with prior-year recommendations still in progress.
findings.matters: A five-year trend of VfM weaknesses across all three criteria suggests the Council's ability to deliver value for money and manage its operations effectively remains fundamentally constrained.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years (2020/21–2024/25) of significant VfM weaknesses identified; three new recommendations in 2024/25
findings.quote: identified significant weaknesses across all three VfM criteria—financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness—for the fifth consecutive year

findings.headline: Internal Audit provides only 'moderate assurance' on governance and control framework, indicating controls are not consistently applied or fully effective across the organisation.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit concluded that whilst key elements of governance, risk management and control framework are in place, their inconsistent application and varying levels of maturity limit overall effectiveness. Audit findings identified that controls are not yet fully embedded in some areas, particularly where processes rely on manual intervention, data quality is variable, or governance arrangements are still maturing.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance is a weak verdict and means financial processing, budget control, and governance processes cannot be relied upon to operate consistently.
findings.figures: Moderate assurance opinion for 2025/26; response rate on effectiveness survey 51.6% (16 of 31 senior officers)
findings.quote: For 2025/26, the opinion is moderate assurance, reflecting that, whilst key elements of the governance, risk management, and control framework are in place, their inconsistent application and varying levels of maturity limit overall effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025 - 2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care has been issued a Section 50 notification by the Department of Health and Social Care for failing to meet statutory duties under the Care Act.
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission assessment (December 2025, published June 2026) concluded Adult Social Care 'requires improvement' and identified weaknesses in system safety, ineffective risk management, delays in assessments and reviews, and fragmented service delivery. Performance on key measures including timeliness of assessments remains below regional and national comparators. The Section 50 notification requires the Council to demonstrate remedial action to the Secretary of State.
findings.matters: A regulatory notification for non-compliance with statutory duties on a major demand-led service indicates systemic operational and governance failure that will consume management attention and may require significant additional investment.
findings.figures: CQC assessment December 2025; performance below regional and national comparators on Adult Social Care Outcomes Framework measures
findings.quote: Nottingham City Council has been issued with a Section 50 notification identifying areas where it is not meeting its statutory duties under the Care Act. The Council is therefore required to demonstrate remedial action to the Secretary of State for the Department of Health and Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025 - 2026
findings.headline: Council issued a Section 114 notice in November 2023 for inability to set a balanced budget; recovery is now early-stage despite achievement of 2026/27 balanced budget without Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: Following a Section 114 notice issued by the then Section 151 Officer due to concerns about financial sustainability, Government appointed Commissioners to oversee recovery. The Council has since improved financial management, reduced reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (only £7.737m used of £41.024m approved in 2024/25), and set a balanced budget for 2026/27. However, the Commissioners' oversight concluded in March 2026, marking the start of the Council managing recovery independently.
findings.matters: Section 114 is a critical threshold event for local authority lending. While recovery progress is welcome, it is very early-stage and dependent on continued financial discipline.
findings.figures: Section 114 issued November 2023; Commissioners oversight concluded March 2026; EFS £41.024m approved 2024/25, only £7.737m required year-end; 2026/27 balanced budget achieved without EFS
findings.quote: In November 2023, a Section 114 (Part 3) report was issued to Councillors due to concerns regarding the financial sustainability of the Council

The Council is undertaking an External Audit improvement programme to restore assurance over accounts and key balances, including reserves, but this work is not yet complete.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing
findings.headline: Treasury Management risk rating remains above target with acknowledged control gaps
findings.detail: The council's own Treasury Management risk register shows a score of 4.23 against a target of 2.94—persistently above acceptable levels. The council acknowledges that 'there are still some improvements that can be made to reduce the risk to target', indicating known weaknesses in treasury controls that have not yet been remediated.
findings.matters: A lender financing local government borrowing needs confidence in the council's treasury risk management. An acknowledged gap between actual and target risk score, with unresolved improvement actions, suggests treasury controls are weaker than they should be and may require tighter monitoring.
findings.figures: Risk rating 4.23 (actual) vs target 2.94; likelihood categorised as 'unlikely' with 'minor' impact, but score is above the target 'remote/minor' threshold

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing
findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorated significantly against budget
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's debt-to-revenue ratio came in at 1.520 against an estimate of 1.050, a variance of 45% worse than forecast. This suggests either the estimate was poor or actual debt repayment/revenue collection did not perform as anticipated. The absolute debt levels did improve (£199.5m actual vs £263m estimate), so the deterioration is driven by lower-than-expected HRA revenue.
findings.matters: HRA sustainability depends on the balance between debt levels and revenue collection. A significant miss in this ratio signals either forecasting weakness or unexpected revenue shortfall in the housing business, both of which affect long-term HRA affordability and the council's ability to service housing debt.
findings.figures: HRA debt £199.5m (against estimate £263.0m), HRA revenues £130.9m (against estimate £130.3m), resulting ratio 1.520 actual vs 1.050 estimate
findings.quote: Ratio of Debt to Revenues 1.050 [estimate] 1.520 [actual]

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing
findings.headline: Council breached its own Treasury Management Strategy counterparty limits
findings.detail: The council held balances above the approved Lloyds Bank counterparty threshold for longer than the four-day allowance permitted in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement. This was done to support debt repayment activity and maintain liquidity during 'heightened uncertainty', but represents an explicit departure from the approved strategy that the council is transparently reporting.
findings.matters: A lender assessing control strength needs to know when a council departs from its own approved controls, even if management claims it was prudent. This indicates either the strategy was too rigid, or controls were not tight enough to enforce in practice.
findings.figures: The breach involved holding balances above the target threshold for an unspecified period longer than four days; the document does not quantify the excess held or for how long.
findings.quote: During the year, the Council departed from its own pre-set Lloyds Bank counterparty limit by holding balances above the target threshold for longer than the four-day allowance set out in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement.

findings.paper_url: https://committee.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/documents/s183978/Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing.pdf
findings.headline: Investment balances declined 28% year-on-year while council relies on £603m internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council held £253.7m in investments at year-end, down from £351.1m (a £97.4m or 28% decrease). This mirrors the council's deliberate strategy of using £603.2m of internal borrowing to fund 44% of its capital financing requirement, avoiding external debt. The council forecasts balances will remain adequate, but the rate of decline may constrain future flexibility.
findings.matters: The council's ability to continue its debt reduction strategy without external borrowing is dependent on maintaining sufficient cash reserves; if balances continue to decline at current rates, the council may face pressure to take external borrowing at less favorable rates or adjust its capital program.
findings.figures: Investments £253.7m (2025/26) vs £351.1m (2024/25), a decline of £97.4m; internal borrowing £603.2m funds 44% of capital financing requirement of £1,153.0m
findings.quote: The Council's internal borrowing position at 31 March 2026 was £603.2m. This meant that approximately 44% of the overall capital borrowing need was not funded with loan debt as cash held by the Council for reserves, balances and cash flow was used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: Tree Services overspend of £0.8m reflects costs of bringing service into legal compliance following safety incident, with ongoing budget pressure
findings.detail: Following a significant tree safety incident at Wollaton Park in 2024, the council implemented a comprehensive tree safety review and new inspection regime. Compliance costs resulted in an £0.8m overspend in 2025/26 for required maintenance and remedial works, and this is flagged as an ongoing pressure.
findings.matters: This reveals deferred maintenance liability that has now crystallised into a budget pressure. The council now carries heightened legal and reputational risk if tree safety standards slip again.
findings.figures: £0.8m overspend on Tree Services in year
findings.quote: A comprehensive review of Tree Services was undertaken in 2024 following a significant tree safety incident at Wollaton Park. This has resulted in a strengthened approach to tree safety management across Highways and Parks, including the implementation of a new Tree Safety Policy and an enhanced inspection regime. While these improvements have brought the service into a legally compliant position, they have also identified a substantial increase in required maintenance and remedial works, resulting in an ongoing budget pressure.

findings.headline: Corporate budget underspend of £34.6m is driven by one-off treasury gains (early debt repayment, investment income) not recurring in future years
findings.detail: The £34.6m underspend in corporate budgets is substantially composed of non-recurring items: £8.5m from early debt repayment discounts, £13.7m from higher treasury investment income, and £7.3m net release of insurance reserves. These mask the true underlying position and will not repeat.
findings.matters: The council's reported underspend relies heavily on one-off financial engineering and windfalls. Removal of these items from future years creates a material budget gap not yet addressed in the medium-term plan.
findings.figures: £8.5m debt repayment savings, £13.7m treasury gains, £7.3m insurance provision release, £34.6m total corporate underspend
findings.quote: Treasury and Capital Financing is underspent by £16.3m. This is mainly due to reduced borrowing costs as a result of a debt restructure exercise optimising interest rate shifts involving a significant repayment of legacy debt with available cash investments.

findings.headline: Savings programme delivering only 80%, with £5.6m at outright risk and future MTFP increasing targets by £5.3m
findings.detail: Of £39.1m approved savings, only £31.1m (80%) were delivered in 2025/26. £6.9m slipped to 2026/27 and £5.6m remain undelivered. The £10.2m workforce savings achieved were largely unplanned, through vacancy management and turnover rather than structured restructuring. Future years will require an additional £5.3m of workforce savings on top of carryforward undelivered targets.
findings.matters: Savings delivery shortfall in year is offset by in-year underspends but signals the council cannot reliably hit targets. Future years stack undelivered savings on top of new ones, compounding the risk of budget failure.
findings.figures: £31.1m delivered of £39.1m target (80%), £6.9m amber/delayed, £5.6m red/at risk, £10.2m achieved via vacancy only
findings.quote: £31.1m (80%) has been delivered in 2025/26, with £6.9m of slippage expected to be delivered in 2026/27 and £5.6m of non-delivered savings programmes. It is to be noted that although the £10.2m cross-cutting workforce savings have been delivered in 2025/26, this is largely via untargeted vacancy management and general turnover.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs reserves depleting unsustainably, with deficit now £3.9m and recovery plan paused
findings.detail: The High Needs block shows a £3.9m deficit. Reserves have fallen sharply from over £21m two years ago to £12.1m now. The council acknowledges this trajectory is not sustainable and projects full depletion within four years without intervention. The DSG High Needs Recovery Plan was developed but then paused pending a national SEND White Paper.
findings.matters: A ringfenced grant deficit that is growing despite intervention signals unmanageable demand pressure. The pause on the recovery plan means no active mitigation is underway, and SEND costs are driven by statutory obligations the council cannot refuse.
findings.figures: £3.9m deficit, reserves £12.1m (down from £21m+), four-year depletion projection
findings.quote: While reserves remain sufficient to cover the in-year deficit of £3.9m, they have reduced materially over the past two years - from over £21m to £12.1m following the 2025/26 outturn. This position is not sustainable. Without intervention, current projections indicate that the deficit will continue to grow over the next four years, fully depleting reserves and potentially resulting in a significant cumulative deficit.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend growing despite falling caseloads, with £9.9m provision for ICB income loss
findings.detail: The Adults and Public Health directorate reports an £11.6m overspend against £89.8m budget. The council has established a £9.9m provision against potential income reduction from the Integrated Care Board, reflecting a contested funding dispute. Despite reducing the number of care packages, average care costs per package continue to rise.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural cost pressure in a statutory service that is not being controlled by volume reductions. The ICB dispute is unresolved and represents contingent liability.
findings.figures: £11.6m overspend, £9.9m ICB provision, £10.7m savings target with only £5.5m delivered (52%)
findings.quote: The overspend includes the prudent recognition of a £9.9m provision in relation to the potential reduction of income due to the new ICB approach for jointly funded care packages. This represents the worst-case scenario; it is not an acceptance of liability. Dispute resolution is ongoing.

findings.committee: East Midlands Shared Services Joint Committee
findings.paper_title: East Midlands Shared Services financial outturn position 2025/26
findings.headline: 2026/27 pay award offer of 3.2% is below budgeted provision of 3.5%, with union negotiations indicating risk of higher outcome
findings.detail: The EMSS budget provision for 2026/27 pay award is 3.5% (£148k). The employers' opening and final offer is 3.2% (£136k). The document states early indications suggest this offer will be rejected and negotiations are ongoing, creating risk that the final award exceeds budget provision.
findings.matters: If the pay award settles above 3.5%, the service will face a budget shortfall with no reserves to absorb it, requiring immediate cost recovery from partner authorities.
findings.figures: Budget provision 3.5% (£148k), employers' offer 3.2% (£136k)
findings.quote: Early indications suggest this offer will be rejected, with negotiations ongoing. Consequently, there remains a risk that the final award may be higher than the provision made in the budget for 2026/27.

findings.committee: East Midlands Shared Services Joint Committee
findings.paper_title: East Midlands Shared Services financial outturn position 2025/26
findings.headline: EMSS reserve fully depleted with no buffer for operational costs or unexpected pressures
findings.detail: The EMSS held reserves historically for redundancy costs, invest-to-save initiatives and exceptional demand. In June 2022 the joint committee approved removal of the reserve due to depletion below best practice. The balance is now fully depleted. Going forward, any operational overspend must be funded 50:50 by the two partner authorities, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Lack of reserves reduces resilience to budget shocks and means any cost overrun must be immediately funded by the councils, constraining their flexibility.
findings.figures: Reserve fully depleted as of 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis.

findings.headline: Children's Services rated Inadequate by Ofsted with DfE Intervention Notice; ongoing improvement required
findings.detail: Following Inadequate judgment in 2022/23, six monitoring visits (April, July, November 2024) have shown overall improvements but 'further work to do'. DfE Intervention Notice triggered sector-led improvement support. Children's Partnership Improvement Board established with DfE independent chair. While trajectory is improving, indicates service delivery and management weakness.
findings.matters: Service inadequacy findings and external intervention signal management weakness; may drive remedial costs and reputational risk affecting council credit standing
findings.figures: Inadequate rating issued 2022/23, six monitoring visits including April, July, November 2024
findings.quote: Following the Inadequate judgement of Nottingham Children's Services in 2022/23 there have been six further monitoring visits Including April, July, November 2024. Each of which have demonstrated overall improvements with further work to do to ensure that we are consistently supporting children and young people in Nottingham City.

findings.headline: Secretary of State appointed Commissioners to oversee council improvement; financial sustainability remains core dependency
findings.detail: Following Section 114, Secretary of State issued Directions on 22 February 2024 and appointed Commissioners. Council developed three-aim Improvement Plan covering financial sustainability, governance, and people/processes. Commissioners report positive progress but specifically advised 'over the coming year the Council will need to move into the implementation phase for these plans to have the required impact'. Implementation delivery is critical to financial recovery.
findings.matters: External oversight by government-appointed Commissioners indicates governance weakness; failure to move plans into implementation phase risks continued financial distress
findings.figures: Commissioners appointed 22 February 2024
findings.quote: Furthermore, the commissioners reported that over the past year, there has been much positive progress on developing plans, strategies, and programmes for improvement such as the Council Plan, Medium Term Financial Plan, and Improvement Plan along with securing and organising the necessary capacity to deliver. The Commissioners also advised that over the coming year; the Council will need to move into the implementation phase for these plans to have the required impact.

findings.headline: Internal audit concluded control environment provides only limited assurance due to staffing and resource constraints
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's opinion for 2024/25 is 'Limited assurance' on the adequacy and effectiveness of the control environment. This assessment is based on fewer reviews than normal due to 'limited resources and various management changes within the function in 2024/25'. The statement acknowledges limited opinion is 'not adequate' but notes signs of improvement in recent reviews.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on internal controls affects confidence in financial data integrity, transaction processing and management's ability to prevent and detect error or fraud
findings.figures: 2024/25 opinion
findings.quote: Due to limited resources and various management changes within the function in 2024/25 there were fewer reviews undertaken in 2024/25. In order to provide an opinion based on sufficient coverage the reviews completed in 2023/24 and 2024/25 were taken into consideration. The overall opinion for 2024/25 is Limited assurance.

findings.headline: External auditors disclaimed the 2023/24 accounts, unable to gain sufficient assurance
findings.detail: Grant Thornton were unable by the statutory deadline to gain the requisite level of assurance on the 2023/24 Accounts and therefore disclaimed them entirely. Only the Value for Money Audit was completed. This is more serious than a qualified audit opinion and prevents reliance on audited financial statements for that year.
findings.matters: Audited accounts are fundamental to financial reporting; disclaimer indicates serious gaps in accounting systems, documentation or governance that auditors could not resolve
findings.figures: 2023/24 financial year
findings.quote: the 2023/24 Accounts were disclaimed as the auditors were unable by the backstop date to gain the requisite level of assurance on the Accounts. However, they were able to complete the Value for Money Audit. This was reported to the Audit Committee in March 2025.

findings.headline: Council required £41m exceptional financial support to set 2024/25 budget and remains under indefinite spending controls
findings.detail: A Section 114 report was issued in November 2023 when the council could not meet its statutory obligation to deliver a balanced budget. The government approved £41.024m of Exceptional Financial Support to 'capitalise' revenue expenditure. By year-end only £7.737m was drawn, but spend control policy has been extended indefinitely from its original March 2025 end date.
findings.matters: Direct evidence of financial crisis and ongoing dependency on exceptional measures; indefinite spending restrictions signal persistent concerns about financial discipline and management
findings.figures: £41.024m EFS approved for 2024/25, £7.737m actually required by year-end
findings.quote: In November 2023, a Section 114 (part 3) report was issued to Councillors due to the financial sustainability of the Council in line with the Local Government Finance Act 1988. The report was for the then Section 151 Officer to formally notify the Council that, in his professional opinion, the Council was unable to meet its statutory requirement to deliver a balanced budget for 2024/25.

findings.detail: Council recorded £33m underspend against 2024/25 budget and forecasts £22m underspend (6% of budget) at Q3 2025/26. Claims this makes it strongest financial performer among English Core Cities for both years.
findings.matters: Demonstrates improved financial control and budget management, with performance exceeding plan rather than slipping into deficit
findings.figures: £33m underspend 2024/25; £22m predicted underspend Q3 2025/26 (6% variance); described as best Core City performance 2024/25

findings.headline: Debt reduced by £0.648bn (60%) from 2020 peak of £1.083bn
findings.detail: Council has cut debt from £1.083bn in 2020 to £0.436bn as of report date. This substantial reduction has decreased financing costs and improved financial resilience and stability.
findings.matters: Major debt reduction directly strengthens council's balance sheet and reduces future servicing burden, a key factor in lending decisions
findings.figures: £0.648bn reduction; debt fell from £1.083bn (2020) to £0.436bn (current)
findings.quote: cut its debt by £0.648bn (approximately 60%) from £1.083bn in 2020 to £0.436bn as of today . This in turn has significantly reduced financing payments and has contributed towards significantly improved financial stability and resilience.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Services under regulatory scrutiny: Ofsted Inadequate rating still active, CQC re-inspection pending, Adult Social Care issues flagged
findings.detail: Ofsted's Inadequate rating for Children's Services (from 2022) remains in place; no formal re-inspection has been published. Four different heads of service in 18 months make improvement more challenging. CQC re-inspected in December 2025 but the report will not be available until March 2026. Adult Social Care inspection in January 2025 identified failings.
findings.matters: Regulatory ratings affect the council's creditworthiness and ability to deliver statutory functions. An Inadequate rating and pending CQC findings create uncertainty and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Ofsted: Inadequate rating from 2022, no re-inspection published yet; four Children's Service heads in 18 months. CQC re-inspection: December 2025, report expected March 2026.
findings.quote: Monitoring visits by Ofsted since 2022 have highlighted evidence of progress, but there have been four different heads of service in the last eighteen months, which makes overall improvement more challenging. As there has been no formal re-inspection published yet, Ofsted's Inadequate rating from 2022 remained in place at the time of writing this report.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Multiple senior leadership changes concurrent with Commissioner oversight; fourth head of Children's Service in 18 months
findings.detail: Since February 2024, Commissioners have overseen all strategic decisions. The council has experienced one change each of Chief Executive, Monitoring Officer, Leader, Deputy Leader, and s151 officer; two changes of Audit Committee Chair; and four different heads of Children's Service in the last 18 months. An independent member was recruited to the Audit Committee in January 2026.
findings.matters: Turnover at this level, especially during Commissioner intervention, disrupts institutional knowledge and continuity. Four heads of Children's Service in 18 months suggests the role is unstable or the council is struggling to retain leadership.
findings.figures: One change each: Chief Executive, Monitoring Officer, Leader, Deputy Leader, s151; two changes of Audit Committee Chair; four different Children's Service heads in last 18 months.
findings.quote: Since 22 February 2024, Commissioners have overseen all functions associated strategic decision making by the Council. There has also been significant turnover at the top of the Council since the end of 2023/24: One change of Chief Executive Officer, Monitoring Officer, Leader, Deputy Leader and s151; two changes of Chair of Audit Committee; two new roles added for Adults & Housing and for Children & Education.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Procurement compliance worsening: exemptions doubled to £20.34m value in one year, £9.278m avoidable
findings.detail: Procurement exemptions increased from 44 requested/33 approved in 2023/24 to 60 requested/54 approved in 2024/25. The total value of exemptions requested for 2024/25 was £20.34m, of which the council estimated £9.278m was avoidable. About 20 waivers occurred because of delays in compliant procurement processes.
findings.matters: Rising exemptions signal breakdown in procurement discipline and compliance. Avoidable exemptions suggest the council is not managing commercial processes properly, risking overpayment and non-competitive procurement.
findings.figures: 2023/24: 44 exemptions requested, 33 approved; 2024/25: 60 requested, 54 approved. Value of exemptions requested 2024/25: £20.34 million; avoidable portion: £9.278 million.
findings.quote: The number of procurement exemptions increased between 2023/24 and 2024/25 from 44 requested / 33 approved, to 60 requested / 54 approved. For 2024/25, the total value of exemptions requested was £20.34 million. Within this, the Council estimated that £9.278 million was avoidable.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support massively overestimated: requested £41.143m for 2024/25, used only £7.737m
findings.detail: The government agreed to advance £41.143m in Exceptional Financial Support for 2024/25 based on the council's forecast. By August 2025, the council estimated it needed only £7.737m—a gap of £33.4m. This reversal indicates the original budget crisis was overstated or resolved faster than expected, but it also shows the council's inability to forecast its own position.
findings.matters: The council drew down far less government support than it anticipated, suggesting either the crisis was misunderstood or the recovery was unexpectedly rapid. Either way, it signals unreliability in the council's financial forecasting to government.
findings.figures: Government agreed-in-principle EFS for 2024/25: £41.143 million; estimated usage by August 2025: £7.737 million; gap: £33.406 million.
findings.quote: In February 2024, the Government confirmed that it was minded to approve the Council's request for EFS of £41.143 million in respect of 2024/25. In February 2025, the Government agreed-in-principle to further EFS requested by the Council of £25 million in respect of 2025/26 and £10 million in respect of 2026/27. By August 2025, the Council was estimating that only £7.737 million of the agreed-in-principal amount for 2024/25 had been needed; less than £10 million was needed in respect of 2025/26; and that nothing would be needed in respect of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Housing stock maintenance backlog of £958 million after 10-year gap in condition survey
findings.detail: The council commissioned its first stock condition survey in a decade and identified that repairs and maintenance costs of £958 million will be needed over a rolling programme to bring housing stock up to standard. A regulatory notice from the Regulator for Social Housing remains active. Tenant satisfaction at end-Q2 2025/26 was 63%, lower than the 67% seen at start of 2023/24 (though recovering from 56% at end of 2023/24).
findings.matters: A £958m maintenance backlog is a massive unfunded liability. The council will need to borrow or find grants to address it, and service quality is affecting tenant confidence.
findings.figures: £958 million repairs and maintenance costs needed over rolling programme; tenant satisfaction 63% (Q2 2025/26), down from 67% (start 2023/24), up from 56% (end 2023/24).
findings.quote: the Council carried out its first stock condition survey for ten years and identified that repairs and maintenance costs of some £958 million will be needed over a rolling programme to bring the stock up to expected standards.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: ICT systems in crisis: no strategy, unknown spend, no business cases, 86 improvement items identified
findings.detail: An independent review in March 2025 found the council's ICT function had no discernible strategy, no business cases, weak asset controls, unapproved cloud application access, and low staff morale. The review made 86 recommendations. The council cannot reliably state its annual ICT spend, estimated at £14.5–16 million. A new permanent Chief Technology Officer was recruited in September 2025 and took post in December 2025.
findings.matters: ICT system failures affect data integrity, operational continuity, and the reliability of all financial and operational information the council produces. Unknown spend and lack of controls are serious governance gaps.
findings.figures: 86 recommendations for improvement; estimated annual ICT spend £14.5–16 million (actual amount unknown); new Head of ICT recruited September 2025, posted December 2025.
findings.quote: business cases were not used for the ICT service; and control over ICT assets and services was weak. The review made 86 recommendations for improvement and noted that there was low morale within the ICT team.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Internal control environment broken: Internal Audit ignored, risk management in infancy, Strategic Risk Register inadequate
findings.detail: The Commissioners found that 'Internal Audit is largely ignored, its reports and recommendations have not been acted on for some time, resulting in a questionable internal control environment.' The Strategic Risk Register is not comprehensive or up to date. Risk management is in its infancy. In April 2025, there were 28 high-priority and 25 medium-priority Internal Audit recommendations outstanding, falling to 13 high and 15 medium by September 2025—but even these reductions are unvalidated.
findings.matters: A questionable internal control environment means risks are not being identified or managed. Controls over expenditure, fraud prevention, and operational reliability are compromised.
findings.figures: April 2025: 28 high-priority and 25 medium-priority audit recommendations outstanding. September 2025: 13 high-priority and 15 medium-priority (unvalidated reduction).
findings.quote: Internal Audit is largely ignored, its reports and recommendations have not been acted on for some time, resulting in a questionable internal control environment. Risk management is in its infancy, although some areas are better than others.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Accounts unaudited for five years; 2024/25 audit incomplete; reserves without external assurance since 2019
findings.detail: Accounts for 2019/20 through 2023/24 all received disclaimed opinions under government backstop arrangements. The 2024/25 audit remains incomplete at the time of this report. Reserves balances—a complex area that includes corrections from an HRA ringfence breach—have had no external audit assurance for five years. The council missed the 2024/25 accounts publication deadline by 11 days.
findings.matters: A lender cannot trust the council's financial position when accounts have gone unaudited for five years. Reserves cannot be verified, and corrections made after the HRA breach remain unaudited. This is a fundamental accountability gap.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions (2019/20–2023/24); 2024/25 audit incomplete; accounts publication deadline missed by 11 days.
findings.quote: Under the Government's backstop arrangements, opinions were disclaimed on the accounts for all years inclusive from 2019/20 to 2023/24. The Council's existing systems, processes, and resources have not been sufficient to support the delivery of the 2024/25 external audit, and our audit of the financial statements remains incomplete.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Savings delivery masked by accounting: 85% target met but actual delivery obscured by employee budget 'cushion'
findings.detail: The council planned £42.398m in savings for 2024/25 and reported delivering £35.974m (85%). However, some planned savings didn't materialize. The shortfall was offset by not holding back budgets for staff vacancies—the Commissioners found 'full budgeting for the establishment posts with very little held back in terms of inevitable vacancies.' This masking means actual savings performance is worse than reported.
findings.matters: If reported savings aren't real, the council's financial position is worse than stated. Undelivered savings from prior years are also being re-profiled forward, compounding the problem.
findings.figures: Planned savings: £42.398 million; delivered: £35.974 million (85%). Transformation savings included £3.109 million rolled over from earlier years due to prior non-delivery.
findings.quote: Commissioners reported to the Secretary of State in August 2025 that, with regard to 2024/25, the 'shortfall was offset by some very significant 'savings' in the employee budget line. In reality, these savings were due to full budgeting for the establishment posts with very little held back in terms of inevitable vacancies.'

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Budget forecasts wildly inaccurate: £171.7m deficit became £4.3m surplus after revisions mid-year
findings.detail: The original 2024/25 budget, published March 2024, forecast a £171.7m medium-term deficit. By October 2025, revised forecasts showed a £4.3m surplus—a swing of £176m. The 2025/26 budget gap fell from £68.957m to £20.793m. The council attributes the errors to unrealistic assumptions in the original budget, requiring major revisions over the course of the year.
findings.matters: Forecasting this poor is a core governance failure and makes financial planning unreliable. A lender needs confidence the council understands its actual position; this audit shows it didn't.
findings.figures: Original forecast deficit: £171.730 million; revised forecast surplus: £4.287 million. Original 2025/26 gap: £68.957 million; revised: £20.793 million.
findings.quote: The Council's view is that the original 2024/25 budget, developed during 2023/24 and published in March 2024, was underpinned by assumptions that have since proved to be unrealistic.

findings.headline: Access to financial data restricted to limited individuals, creating dependencies and operational risk.
findings.detail: Financial and transactional data access is restricted to a limited number of individuals across multiple systems, creating dependencies on specific personnel. Absences due to annual leave and sickness have resulted in delays obtaining critical information. The auditors note this creates operational risk as key data may be inaccessible during critical periods and may indicate loss of corporate knowledge.
findings.matters: Restricted access to financial systems indicates weak segregation of duties and creates fraud risk. Dependencies on individuals rather than systems mean financial information becomes unavailable when people are absent, threatening business continuity.
findings.figures: Issue identified across multiple systems
findings.quote: In addition, access to financial and transactional data is restricted to a limited number of individuals, creating dependencies on specific personnel. This issue has arisen across multiple systems, not just the Council's main general ledger. Absences due to annual leave and sickness have resulted in delays in obtaining critical information or passing it through central finance for validation before submission to the audit team. These constraints not only impact timeliness and efficiency but also introduces operational risk, as key data may be inaccessible during critical periods.

findings.headline: Unlawful HRA ringfencing breach from 2021 remains unresolved; cannot confirm if management override.
findings.detail: In December 2021 the Interim Chief Finance Officer issued a s114 notice after discovering the council had unlawfully breached the ringfencing requirement for the Housing Revenue Account over seven years, including 2019/20, 2020/21 and 2021/22. Five years later, auditors still cannot establish whether management override of controls caused this breach or whether other similar instances could have occurred.
findings.matters: An unresolved breach of legal ringfencing requirements, combined with inability to determine if it was caused by override or systematic weakness, indicates either weak controls or management misconduct. Either way it suggests past financial statements may be unreliable.
findings.figures: Seven-year breach period including 2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22; s114 notice issued December 2021
findings.quote: In December 2021, the then Interim Chief Finance Officer issued a s114 notice after discovering that the Council had unlawfully breached the ring-fencing requirement for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) over a period of seven years, including the 2019/20, 2020/21 and 2021/22 financial years.

findings.headline: Significant VFM weaknesses across all three criteria; auditors not satisfied council has proper arrangements.
findings.detail: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness; financial sustainability; and governance. The auditors concluded they are not satisfied the council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources for 2024/25.
findings.matters: A formal finding that the council lacks proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness questions whether it can be trusted to spend borrowed money wisely or manage its finances prudently.
findings.figures: Significant weaknesses in all three VFM criteria areas
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements across all three specified criteria. We are therefore not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources for the financial year under review.

findings.headline: Management override of controls risk remains unresolved; auditors unable to obtain assurance it is absent.
findings.detail: The auditors were unable to obtain sufficient assurance that management override of controls is absent from the financial statements. This follows the same concern from prior years. They were unable to complete planned procedures to understand what actions the council has taken to address control environment issues previously identified, including the unlawful HRA ringfencing breach and high error volumes.
findings.matters: Management override of controls is a fundamental fraud risk. The council's inability or unwillingness to demonstrate controls prevent override indicates weak governance. This directly affects whether the accounts can be trusted.
findings.figures: Issue present continuously since 2019/20 audit
findings.quote: We have been unable to obtain sufficient assurance that management override of controls is absent within the financial statements. Due to the material and pervasive nature of the issue, we intend to continue to report this matter in the disclaimer of opinion.

findings.headline: £122.5m dwelling rents income and other material balances lack system support.
findings.detail: The council has been unable to provide detailed supporting listings from its core financial system or subsidiary systems for material balances. A significant example is £122.5m of dwelling rents income, which auditors were unable to commence work on pending an appropriate report. Other unsupported balances include £3.5m enforcement receivables and £2.9m managing agent property charges receivables.
findings.matters: Material income balances without system-generated supporting documentation indicate weak financial systems or data integrity issues. This creates operational risk and prevents verification of the council's asset and revenue position.
findings.figures: Dwelling rents £122.5m, enforcement receivables £3.5m, managing agent charges £2.9m
findings.quote: There are material balances and adjustments within the financial statements for which the Council has been unable to provide detailed supporting listings from its core financial system or supporting subsidiary systems. A significant example is the £122.5 million of income relating to dwelling rents, which we have been unable to commence work on, pending the provision of an appropriate report.

findings.headline: £10m income adjustments in March 2025 lack sufficient supporting evidence.
findings.detail: The council processed approximately £10m of adjustments increasing income and debtors at year-end, with the largest being a £6.129m HRA rental income adjustment in March 2025 to correct an imbalance in the housing rents system. The auditors state they were unable to gain sufficient appropriate assurance over the year-end balances and cannot confirm the adjustments were the appropriate corrections.
findings.matters: Unexplained, unsupported material adjustments at year-end raise fraud and accounting accuracy risks. A lender cannot trust the revenue line without evidence these corrections are valid.
findings.figures: £10m total adjustments, of which £6.129m HRA rental income
findings.quote: The Council has processed adjustments of approximately £10m which increase income and debtors. The largest of these adjustments was posted in March 2025 to correct an imbalance between the housing rents system arrears and the balance in the Council's balance sheet. This had the effect of increasing HRA rental income by £6.129m in 2024/25. We have been informed that these transactions were made following a review of the balance sheet as at 31 March 2025, however in each instance we have not been able to gain sufficient, appropriate assurance over the year-end balance.

findings.headline: Audit unable to complete work in any area of the 2024/25 accounts.
findings.detail: Audit fieldwork commenced July 2025 but the auditors have been unable to conclude their work in any area. They report that as of March 2026, their substantive audit findings are extremely limited, primarily due to lack of progress. Multiple areas lack key information, responses to significant queries have not been received, and critical evidence remains outstanding despite efforts by the council's finance team.
findings.matters: An audit unable to conclude on ANY balance means the financial statements cannot be relied upon for lending decisions or performance assessment. The council's true financial position is unknown.
findings.figures: Audit commenced July 2025, unable to conclude by March 2026 backstop date
findings.quote: Our audit fieldwork commenced in July 2025. We have been unable to conclude our audit work in any area of the accounts.

findings.headline: Dramatic recovery from financial crisis, but future years depend on savings assumptions not yet detailed
findings.detail: Projected MTFP deficit halved from £171m (March 2024/25 MTFP) to £37m; exceptional funding support dropped from £41m projected need to £7.8m actual in 2024/25; 2025/26 Q3 forecast shows £1m surplus and 2026/27 budget projects same. Officer states 'trajectory of improvement...can be fully sustained' but this assumes new savings will be introduced 2027/28-2029/30 as part of normal budget setting.
findings.matters: The recovery is genuine and impressive, demonstrating changed management capability; but the MTFP only balances to 2026/27 if future years' savings materialize, creating execution dependency that extends into years not yet detailed.
findings.figures: Deficit £171m to £37m; EFS need £41m to £7.8m actual; £1m General Fund surplus projected both 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: In 2024, the Council projected a funding gap requirement of £41m to be met by Exceptional Financial Support for 2024/25 but only required £7.8m. The 2025/26 forecast outturn as at Quarter 3 currently assumes no requirement for EFS and against a budget gap set of £20.8m, the Council will fully eliminate such a gap and record a surplus of £1m by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: £28m earmarked for Local Government Reorganisation creates uncertain reserve exposure
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves include £28m provision for estimated LGR transitional costs, allocated from what was previously unallocated reserves. If LGR proceeds and costs exceed this estimate, additional funds would have to come from unallocated reserves already at statutory minimum.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change with uncertain costs; cost overruns would directly erode already-tight reserves, forcing either policy breach or further savings acceleration.
findings.figures: £28m LGR provision; earmarked reserves £188.3m of which this is material allocation
findings.quote: Given the likely LGR transitional cost liabilities estimated by advisers as £28m, such an allocation of 'unallocated' reserve is considered to be prudent.

findings.headline: Officer's positive approval is conditional on council stopping use of reserves to cover recurring revenue spending
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly conditions his robust opinion on the council not calling on reserves to meet ongoing service costs or growth, only for identified risks. This indicates past practice of using one-off reserves to plug budget gaps; the officer is tightening this off to preserve reserves.
findings.matters: If the council has previously used reserves to mask recurring spending pressures, the stated robustness of the budget is fragile; the officer's conditions suggest this practice must stop, implying stronger discipline will be needed going forward.
findings.figures: No specific numbers; this is a policy condition
findings.quote: Not considering further calls on reserves to meet service growth or recurring expenditure other than for those risks that have been identified, those that could not have been reasonably foreseen and those risks that cannot be dealt with through management or policy actions.

findings.headline: Unallocated reserves now at statutory minimum 10% (£46.7m), down from £63.5m in 2024/25
findings.detail: General Fund unallocated reserves have fallen £16.8m in two years to exactly 10% of net expenditure. The Section 151 Officer cannot recommend below this floor; any further deterioration would breach reserves policy, leaving no headroom for unforeseen costs or savings shortfalls.
findings.matters: A council at its minimum safe reserve level has no buffer; if 2026/27 savings delivery repeats 2025/26's 68% rate, a £10m+ gap would force an emergency draw on reserves, breaching policy and signalling financial distress.
findings.figures: £46.7m unallocated 2026/27 at 10% minimum; down from £63.5m in 2024/25; earmarked reserves £188.3m but allocated for specific purposes
findings.quote: To reflect the challenging operating environment and related financial risks, the Section 151 Officer recommends that the Council maintains a minimum unallocated General Fund balance at a level of at least 10% of net expenditure.

findings.headline: High-risk existing savings commitments concentrated in Adult Social Care (£1.6m) and Finance (£1.6m)
findings.detail: Table 3 shows £4.832m of existing MTFP savings rated high-risk of non-delivery, reflecting that multi-year commitments from prior budgets are proving harder to achieve than expected. Adult Social Care faces £1.628m high-risk existing savings plus £1.5m Target Operating Model savings, a demand-led service now under pressure.
findings.matters: Multi-year savings slippage signals prior-year budget assumptions were optimistic; councils that cannot deliver promised savings struggle with financial control; demand-led services facing savings cuts may face cost spikes if demand rises.
findings.figures: £4.832m high-risk existing savings total; Adult Social Care £1.628m high-risk, £1.5m TOM savings; Children's & Education £1.430m (all high-risk); Finance & Resources £1.564m high-risk
findings.quote: The difficulty in delivering the 2026/27 savings carried forward from previous years naturally provides a higher risk of full delivery in 2026/27. A large proportion of these savings are the second year of the workforce savings, but Adult Social Care also have Target Operating Model savings of £1.5m relating to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council must deliver £33.3m annual savings, but £12m already missed 2025/26 deadline
findings.detail: Table 4 shows £11.989m of 2025/26 savings targets carried forward to 2026/27 because they were not achieved. The council completed only 68% of 2025/26 savings by Q3. This means the largest-ever annual savings target includes savings already proven difficult to hit, raising execution risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can deliver the savings it depends on; carrying forward misses from the prior year and taking them on again alongside new targets materially increases shortfall risk.
findings.figures: £33.278m 2026/27 total (£11.189m new + £10.100m existing + £11.989m delayed); 68% delivery rate on 2025/26 savings (£13.201m delivered of £39.135m target)
findings.quote: The council also has £12m of delayed savings in 2025/26 – see table 4 below. All savings in 2025/26 that are not delivered were assessed at 50% likelihood of delivery in 2026/27 to account for any future possible delays.

findings.matters: A material reserve drawdown for reorganisation costs will significantly reduce financial resilience at a time when local government is under stress and when the council faces a multi-year structural deficit.
