findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £37.1m over four years with no savings identified for 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget shows a £1.063m surplus, but the council faces a projected cumulative budget gap of £37.107m over the 4-year MTFP without new savings identified for years 2027/28 to 2029/30. The council aspirationally targets £50m in savings (£10m, £20m, £20m across the later years) but these are not yet approved or detailed.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a projected multi-year deficit has a credible delivery plan, but none exists yet for £37m of required savings.
findings.figures: £37.107m cumulative gap; 2026/27 surplus £1.063m; £50m aspirational savings target
findings.quote: Notes that the Council has a projected cumulative budget gap of £37.107m over the 4-year MTFP period without new savings being identified for years 2027/28 to 2029/30

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support budgeted to balance 2025/26 but now not required, signalling underlying budget gap
findings.detail: The council's 2025/26 budget was approved incorporating £20.8m of Exceptional Financial Support (financed from capital receipts) to balance the budget. Due to forecast underspends, this is no longer required for this year. However, the baseline budget gap signals structural pressures that remain unresolved in future years' MTFP.
findings.matters: Reliance on EFS and capital receipts to balance budgets is not sustainable; the existence of the gap indicates the council's MTFP contains unresolved funding challenges for future years
findings.figures: £20.8m EFS budgeted; £0m forecast required; £1.6m projected underspend on break-even basis
findings.quote: To note the General Fund budget includes a budget gap of £20.8m which was scheduled to be met through the application of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), which would be financed through use of capital receipts. However, due to the level of forecasted underspend, the projected EFS of £20.8m is no longer required.

findings.headline: HRA overspend of £1.5m driven by £7.9m provision for damp, mould and legal disrepair works
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is overspending by £1.5m. The main driver is £7.9m of pressures for damp, mould and Legal Disrepair works arising from a stock condition survey and legal disrepair process. These costs were budgeted in the capital programme but are properly chargeable to revenue. HRA reserves will be drawn down to £4.8m contribution, up from the budgeted £3.3m.
findings.matters: The need to charge £7.9m of asset works to revenue signals emerging asset condition risks; growing HRA reserve drawdown reduces financial flexibility and raises questions about the adequacy of the capital programme for asset maintenance
findings.figures: £1.5m HRA overspend; £7.9m damp, mould and disrepair provision; £0.7m void property repair overspend; HRA reserve contribution rising to £4.8m from £3.3m budgeted
findings.quote: £7.9m pressure for damp and mould related HHSRS (Housing, Health & Safety Rating System) and Legal Disrepair works work arising from a stock condition survey and the legal disrepair process. Some of these costs were previously budgeted for in the capital programme. However, these costs are properly chargeable to revenue

findings.headline: DSG High Needs running £7.9m in-year deficit with planned deficits through 2027/28
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs service is forecast to run a £7.9m deficit in 2025/26, followed by further deficits in 2026/27 (£3.3m) and 2027/28 (£0.3m). Reserves are being drawn down from £14.6m opening balance to just £3.1m by end of 2027/28. The document notes this 'takes no account of the potential impact of Government's reforms on DSG/SEND provision or Local Government Reorganisation.'
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a statutory concern and signal structural underfunding of SEND provision; continued deficits through the medium term erode reserves and reduce financial flexibility for other pressures
findings.figures: £7.9m 2025/26 deficit; £3.3m 2026/27 deficit; £0.3m 2027/28 deficit; opening reserves £14.6m declining to £3.1m by 2027/28
findings.quote: As per above table, the council expects to run a £7.9m deficit in 2025/26, leading to a residual £6.7m closing reserve balance. After further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, it anticipates moving back in-year surpluses.

findings.headline: Adults and Public Health overspend of £13.1m driven by external care demand and undelivered savings
findings.detail: The directorate is overspending by £13.1m against a £90.1m budget, with external care packages overspending by £4.5m across all service user groups (older people £1.8m, physical disability £2.3m, learning disabilities £0.6m). The service is delivering only 53% of its £10.7m savings target. The document identifies this as structural, driven by rising demand and increasing complexity of citizen needs.
findings.matters: Adult social care represents material budget impact and pressures are structural rather than one-off; rising care package volumes (10,307 total) indicate demand is growing, not stabilising
findings.figures: £13.1m overspend; £4.5m external care package overspend; 10,307 total care packages (3,560 older people, 2,731 learning disabilities, 2,465 physical disability, 1,551 mental health); only £5.7m of £10.7m savings forecast to be delivered in-year
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures, impacting its ability to meet the rising demand for services. This is driven by an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs.

findings.headline: Only 68% of £39.1m savings target expected to be delivered in-year, with £12.4m not expected to be delivered
findings.detail: The council targeted £39.1m of savings for 2025/26 but now forecasts delivering only £26.7m (68%). Of the undelivered amount, £12m is delayed to 2026/27 and £5.1m represents non-delivery. The council is mitigating the shortfall with over £10m of staffing vacancies, which is not a sustainable strategy.
findings.matters: Savings miss of this scale indicates budget assumptions are fragile; reliance on vacancy management is not a reliable mitigation and leaves the council exposed if recruitment proceeds as planned
findings.figures: £39.1m savings target; £26.7m (68%) forecast to be delivered; £12m delayed to 2026/27; £5.1m non-delivered; £10m+ staffing vacancies relied upon as mitigation
findings.quote: The council forecasts to achieve £26.7m out of £39.1m in savings in 2025/26, which means that £12.4m is not expected to be delivered and the forecast relies on mitigations, including over £10m of staffing vacancies.

findings.headline: £9m provision for integrated care board reduction in jointly funded care placement funding
findings.detail: The council is recognising a £9m worst-case provision for potential reductions in ICB funding for jointly funded care packages. The document explicitly states this is 'not an acceptance of liability' and that 'dispute resolution is ongoing', but the council is adopting a 'prudent approach' and provisioning at the conservative end of the spectrum due to year-end proximity.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could worsen if the dispute proceeds unfavourably; it represents a structural change in how jointly funded care is financed that will affect future years regardless of dispute outcome
findings.figures: £9m provision in 2025/26; £9m income shortfall in Mental Health and Whole Life Disability service; total external care package overspend of £4.5m
findings.quote: Within this overspend the council is prudently recognising a £9m provision in relation to the potential reduction of income due to the new ICB approach in relation to jointly funded care placements. This provision represents the worst-case scenario and is not an acceptance of liability and dispute resolution is ongoing

findings.headline: 40.6% of remaining debt matures in 25–40 years, creating a refinancing wall around 2050–2065 that current financial strategy does not yet address.
findings.detail: Table 15 shows maturity structure. The upper threshold for borrowing maturing in the 25–40 year bucket is 40.6% of debt. Section 1.15 notes 'the Council reviewed its maturity thresholds accordingly' after the £300m+ reduction, but the concentration in this mid-range maturity bucket means a significant wall of loans will need refinancing simultaneously in ~30 years' time. Section 6.19 acknowledges the importance: 'this matters because it is important to ensure that the council does not re-finance too much of its portfolio.'
findings.matters: Maturity concentration creates refinancing risk. If interest rates are elevated or credit markets are tight in 2050–2065, the council may face forced repricing of 40% of its debt base at once. Long-term fiscal planning should address this, but current strategy focuses on shorter-term reserve management.
findings.figures: 40.6% of debt matures 25–40 years hence; 24.4% matures 10–25 years; only 7.1% under 5 years
findings.quote: the upper threshold for borrowing maturing within 25 to 40 years now represents 40.6% of its debt

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account debt-to-revenues ratio at 114% for 2025/26 (declining only to 82% by 2029/30) signals constrained housing investment capacity.
findings.detail: Table 13 shows HRA debt of £148.9m against revenues of £130.3m (2025/26), implying the HRA borrows roughly its own annual income in debt service and capital needs. While improving, 82% debt-to-revenues (2029/30) leaves little room for expansion or new supply. The HRA is highly geared and any deterioration in rental income or increase in repairs costs could be problematic.
findings.matters: HRA debt is secured on housing assets and tenants' rents. High leverage constrains the council's ability to respond to housing need, including affordable housing supply. For a lender, high HRA gearing suggests limited flexibility and concentration risk in a single service.
findings.figures: HRA debt £148.9m (2025/26); HRA revenues £130.3m; ratio 114.25%; declining to 82.06% by 2029/30
findings.quote: Debt (£m)  148.855  Revenues (£m) 130.290  Ratio of Debt to Revenues (%) 114.25%

findings.headline: Commercial property investment portfolio of £212.1m (mostly borrowed) earning only £9.3m net income; council actively seeking to divest.
findings.detail: Table 24 lists 18+ commercial projects (dubbed Project Doncaster, Project Mulberry, etc.) totalling £212.1m purchase price, of which £208.1m was financed by borrowing. Section 10.5 states 'The Council regularly reviews its investments to identify opportunities for divestment, helping to reduce debt more quickly and support delivery of the Voluntary Debt Reduction policy.' The low net income (£9.334m forecast for 2025/26) suggests either underperforming assets or heavy depreciation charges. No new commercial investments permitted.
findings.matters: If these regeneration/property assets are underperforming, forced sales to raise cash could occur at cyclical lows. Fire-sale asset disposals typically signal financial distress. A lender needs to know whether the £212m is performing, whether write-downs are likely, and whether the council has flexibility to hold underperforming assets through cycles.
findings.figures: £212.1m commercial investments; £208.1m financed by borrowing; £9.334m forecast net income 2025/26; no new commercial investments permitted
findings.quote: The Council regularly reviews its investments to identify opportunities for divestment, helping to reduce debt more quickly and support delivery of the Voluntary Debt Reduction policy.

findings.headline: Capital spending rationed to £52m by 2029/30 (down 74% from current levels) because no new borrowing is permitted except in emergencies.
findings.detail: The Voluntary Debt Reduction Policy from section 12.3 states: 'For the period 2025/26 to 2029/30, no new schemes are to be financed by borrowing.' Table 1 shows capital programme collapsing from £199.6m (2024/25 actual) to £52.4m (2029/30 est). This constraint is independent of project merit or service need.
findings.matters: A five-year capital freeze signals the council is managing cash-flow distress, not strategic choice. Underfunded capital creates deferred maintenance, equipment obsolescence, and service degradation that eventually cost more to fix. For regeneration and economic development, it signals retreat.
findings.figures: Capital spending: £199.6m (2024/25) down to £52.4m (2029/30); no new borrowing permitted 2025/26-2029/30
findings.quote: For the period 2025/26 to 2029/30, no new schemes are to be financed by borrowing.

findings.headline: Council repaid £287m of debt in 2025/26 and is now drawing down reserves to fund the under-borrowed position—expected to hit negative investment balances by 2027/28.
findings.detail: The council undertook two large debt repayments: £89m in August 2025 and £198m in December 2025, reducing gross debt from £741.8m to £435.7m in a single year. Table 5 shows expected investments declining from £351.1m (actual 2024/25) to £109.9m (2025/26 est) to negative £26.1m by 2027/28, meaning the council will need to borrow to meet normal operations unless reserves can be supplemented by asset sales.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's cash runway and whether this aggressive strategy is sustainable. Once reserves hit limits, the no-new-borrowing policy may need to break, or the council may be forced to cut services or sell assets at disadvantageous times.
findings.figures: £287m debt repayment in 2025/26; usable reserves projected to fall from £456.9m (2024/25) to £317.8m (2028/29); expected investments turning negative (negative £26.1m by 2027/28)
findings.quote: The Council is currently under‑borrowed, meaning it is using its own cash (reserves and working capital) instead of taking out new loans. No new General Fund or Housing Revenue Account borrowing is expected during the forecast period.

findings.headline: £212m commercial property portfolio generates £10.6m annual revenue but exposed to market downturn
findings.detail: Commercial property investments total £212m (purchase price), capital value £200.554m at 31 March 2025, funded by £208m of unsupported borrowing. These generate £10.552m net annual revenue to the General Fund (4.52% yield). The council explicitly acknowledges exposure to market risks including downturns, voids, lease breaks and wider economic pressures. Asset sales planned for 2026/27 to reduce debt.
findings.matters: General Fund revenue budget is materially dependent on £10.6m annual yield from properties; any market downturn, vacancy spike, or lease break would directly squeeze budget balance and debt reduction targets.
findings.figures: £212m investment, £200.554m capital value, £10.552m forecast 2025/26 net revenue, 4.52% yield
findings.quote: The gross investment of £222.812m (excluding MRP to 31 March 2025) exposes the Council to market risks such as downturns, voids, lease breaks and wider economic pressures.

findings.headline: £19m essential asset maintenance backlog added to capital programme
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £19m of urgent works to address core fabric issues in council-owned assets. The council explicitly describes these as non-transformational works aimed solely at preventing further asset deterioration, not enhancing value or performance.
findings.matters: Allocation signals underlying condition problems in the council estate; deferring these works would lead to accelerating deterioration costs and potential service disruption.
findings.figures: £19m allocated to urgent maintenance works in current programme
findings.quote: The Capital Programme includes £19m of urgent works to address core fabric issues in Council assets, preventing higher future costs if delayed. These works are not transformational and do not enhance building value or performance; they simply prevent further deterioration.

findings.headline: £37.5m of approved capital schemes removed from programme due to lack of funding
findings.detail: Pipeline schemes totalling £37.502m have been reclassified as temporarily decommissioned and placed outside the capital programme due to unavailable funding. The council acknowledges risks relating to these unfunded schemes are escalating with potential knock-on implications for service delivery.
findings.matters: Service delivery risks are acknowledged as increasing; council cannot fund schemes it identifies as necessary, signalling financial constraint is worse than headline figures suggest.
findings.figures: £37.502m in decommissioned/pipeline schemes
findings.quote: It is recognised that the risks of not incorporating these schemes into the Capital Programme are increasing and may have knock on implications for service delivery.

findings.headline: Council must generate £28.4m from asset sales to fund its approved capital programme
findings.detail: The five-year capital programme (2025/26–2029/30) requires £81.167m of capital receipts. While £52.744m is already available, the council must generate an additional £28.423m through property disposals. This creates material execution risk: if property sales slip or property values fall short, capital schemes will require deferral or cancellation.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery depends entirely on meeting asset sales targets at sufficient values; shortfalls will force service cuts or project delays.
findings.figures: £81.167m capital receipts required, £52.744m available, £28.423m shortfall
findings.quote: The current capital programme requires £81.167m of capital receipts. £52.744m are already available in 2025/26 and it needs to generate £28.423m more to fill the gap.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing prohibition continues beyond 2026/27 despite end of government support
findings.detail: Council issued a Section 114 report in November 2023 due to budget imbalance and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for 2023/24 and 2024/25 with an associated prohibition on capital borrowing. Although the EFS requirement ends in 2026/27, the borrowing prohibition will remain while the council strengthens its financial position.
findings.matters: Even as crisis support ends, the council remains unable to borrow for capital investment, forcing reliance on a fully-funded capital programme and eliminating growth options.
findings.figures: EFS received 2023/24 to 2024/25; prohibition continues indefinitely
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the requirement for EFS has ended but the prohibition remains, while the council strengthens its financial position.

findings.headline: Children's services carries prior-year £4.4m overspend while transformation programme started in April 2025; Ofsted rated Inadequate in 2022
findings.detail: Children's & Education is forecasting £1.6m overspend but this sits on top of a £4.4m prior-year overspend that remains outstanding. The transformation programme started from scratch in April 2025. Children's Regulatory Services alone is overspending by £3.0m. The service received an Ofsted Inadequate rating in 2022; next full inspection is anticipated in 2025. External placement market risks include higher costs and shortage of suitable placements.
findings.matters: An Ofsted Inadequate rating is a governance red flag. The prior-year overspend plus current pressures plus a transformation programme that has only just begun suggests fundamental management capacity issues. External inspection is imminent.
findings.figures: £1.6m current overspend; £4.4m prior-year overspend; £3.0m Children's Regulatory Services overspend; Ofsted rated Inadequate 2022
findings.quote: This reflects a directorate that started its transformation programme from a standing start in April 2025, and an overhanging prior year overspend of £4.4m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant forecasting £4.5m annual deficit with reserve falling to £8.9m after DfE funding cut
findings.detail: DSG is forecasting a £4.5m deficit for 2025/26. The DfE has just announced a £2.7m reduction in the High Needs Allocation (based on lower Published Admission Numbers), leaving a closing reserve of only £8.9m. A full DSG Recovery Plan is being brought forward but has not yet been approved. At the current deficit rate, the reserve will be exhausted in two years.
findings.matters: This is a structural High Needs Block deficit, not a temporary variance. Reserves are the only buffer; they are finite. The DfE has just cut funding, not increased it.
findings.figures: £4.5m annual deficit; £8.9m closing reserve (down from £16.0m opening); £2.7m DfE funding reduction
findings.quote: The DSG contained within the Children's & Education Directorate is forecasting a deficit of £4.5m for 2025/26 with an estimated closing reserve balance of £8.9m.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care is £3.9m (4.1%) over budget with rising external care costs and demand-driven structural pressures
findings.detail: ASC overspend is across external care: Learning Disabilities £1.2m, Mental Health £0.4m, Physical Disability £0.9m, Older People £0.5m. Additionally there is a £2.4m shortfall on Continuing Care and client contributions. The report states the directorate is "experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures" driven by "an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs." Risks flagged include National Living Wage rises, inflationary pressures, and provider exits shrinking market capacity.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off variance but a structural demand issue tied to demographics. The aging population will not reverse. External care price inflation and market tightness are accelerating, not temporary.
findings.figures: £3.9m overspend (4.1% of £94.0m budget); external care overspends £3.1m total
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures, impacting its ability to meet the rising demand for services. This is driven by an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs.

findings.headline: £12.4m of the £39.1m savings target (32%) is not expected to be delivered in-year or at all
findings.detail: The budget was built on £39.1m savings, but only £26.7m (68%) is forecast to be delivered. Of the shortfall, £12.2m is delayed and £5.1m is red-flagged as non-delivery. The reported underspend masks this gap with over £10m of staffing vacancies and 'mitigations', creating an unsustainable reliance on holding posts open.
findings.matters: Vacancies cannot provide permanent cover for structural savings failure. When posts are filled, the £10m+ gap will reappear. This suggests either the savings plans were unachievable or delivery governance is weak.
findings.figures: £39.1m target; £26.7m delivered/on track (68%); £12.4m not expected in-year
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget includes savings of £39.1m of which £26.7m (68%) are delivered or on track to be delivered in 2025/26, but which also indicates that there are £12.4m not expected to be delivered in-year or at all.

findings.headline: £7.0m emerging liability for damp and mould repairs in council housing stock, up £4.5m from Q1
findings.detail: HRA repairs and maintenance is forecasting £6.7m overspend, driven by damp and mould works from a stock condition survey and legal disrepair process. The pressure increased by £4.5m from Q1 when Category 2 damp (respiratory risk) was added to the survey scope. These costs are properly chargeable to revenue and will force additional draw-down of HRA reserves.
findings.matters: This signals unquantified further liabilities in the housing stock beyond Q2. HRA reserves are already being depleted by £6.4m this year to cover this overspend; ongoing damp liability threatens longer-term financial sustainability of the housing service.
findings.figures: £7.0m pressure (£4.5m increase from Q1)
findings.quote: A £7.0m pressure for damp and mould related HHSRS (Housing, Health & Safety Rating System) and Legal Disrepair works work arising from a stock condition survey and the legal disrepair process. This reflects an increase of £4.5m from the Q1 position.

findings.headline: £9.3m risk from Integrated Care Board income reductions not included in the forecast position
findings.detail: Adults & Public Health faces planned ICB funding reductions for jointly funded care placements. The report explicitly states this risk "is not contained within the forecast figures." The risk is assessed as being between £0.0m and £9.3m, depending on how many assessments/eligibility reviews result in reduced placements.
findings.matters: If realized, this £9.3m unforecasted loss would wipe out most of the council's reported £14.6m underspend, turning it into a £1.5m overspend. This is not a contingency, but a known and ongoing issue.
findings.figures: £9.3m risk range
findings.quote: there is still the £9.3m risk from ICB income reductions within the Adults & Public Health Directorate that is not contained within the forecast

findings.headline: Internal audit coverage was significantly reduced in 2024/25 due to resource constraints
findings.detail: The council experienced resource issues that resulted in much-reduced audit coverage in 2024/25, requiring audits from 2023/24 to be included in reaching the annual opinion. This means fewer audit reviews were conducted of the council's systems and controls during the current financial year.
findings.matters: Reduced internal audit coverage weakens assurance over the control environment and increases the risk that control failures or governance issues will not be detected during the financial year.
findings.figures: Specific numbers on audit coverage reduction not disclosed in the available sections
findings.quote: Due to resources issue and therefore a much-reduced coverage in 2024/25, the audits undertaken in 2023/24 have been included in reaching this assessment

editorial.headline: Nottingham City audit opinion disclaimed as joint venture reserves depleted
editorial.standfirst: Depleted reserves in a 50:50 partnership and governance weaknesses have left the council without financial buffer or clean audit bill.
editorial.body:
Nottingham City Council faces a compounding set of financial and governance pressures that have left it without the reserves to absorb further shocks.

The council is a 50:50 partner in East Midlands Shared Services. As of 31 March 2026, EMSS reserves were fully depleted. The council's papers presented to June's joint committee meeting state: "The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis." This leaves Nottingham City liable for half of any cost overrun.

A month later, Grant Thornton, the council's external auditor, issued a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts—a rare step indicating it cannot form a view on the reliability of the financial statements. The council's papers presented to July's corporate scrutiny committee describe the work underway: "Council works closely with the External Auditor to identify the key information and evidential requirements that the auditor will need to provide a positive non-qualified audit opinion from a standard base disclaimed opinion."

But internal audit tells a deeper story. As of 31 July, the Head of Internal Audit's annual opinion for 2025/26 provides only Moderate Assurance. The audit committee papers state: "Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas." Multiple service areas remain problematic. The papers identify Adult Social Care performance and statutory compliance as an ongoing governance issue. Children's Services and Housing Services require continued improvement. Workforce capacity and resilience are constrained.

Compounding these issues is a pay award pressure. The council budgeted 3.5%, but the employers' current offer stands at 3.2%. The EMSS papers note: "Early indications suggest this offer will be rejected, with negotiations ongoing. Consequently, there remains a risk that the final award may be higher than the provision made in the budget for 2026/27."

The combination—zero reserves, audit failure, governance weaknesses not yet embedded—leaves little room for manoeuvre if budget pressures intensify.
editorial.pull_quote: Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas
editorial.watch_next: Grant Thornton is targeting a non-qualified audit opinion by March 2028, when the council's remediation efforts must demonstrate concrete results.
